sentences.text: Galahadosuchus is a genus of saltoposuchid crocodylomorph that lived in the Late Triassic.
Its forearm bones include a radiale and an ulnare that are each about one-tenth the length of the corresponding radius and ulna, giving the hand a short and stout appearance.
The head of the femur points medially, a feature that suggests an erect posture by limiting hind-limb motion to a parasagittal (forward-backward) plane.
Unlike its relatives, the proximal carpals are not elongated, implying they did not primarily support body weight and that the hand may have been more flexible.
The first and fifth metacarpals are shortened, indicating that only the three central digits bore the animal’s weight on the ground.
Researchers have proposed that Galahadosuchus could have been faster than the closely related Terrestrisuchus and possessed more flexible hands.
Limb-proportion analyses place Galahadosuchus among quadrupedal forms, yet it plots slightly nearer to bipedal taxa than Terrestrisuchus does.
Fossils of Galahadosuchus come from the Late Triassic fissure deposits of Cromhall Quarry in the United Kingdom.
The holotype specimen, catalogued as NHMUK PV R 10002, was recovered by Ron Croucher in 1969 from site 1 of those fissure deposits.
That same specimen was formally described as the new species Galahadosuchus jonesi, establishing a new genus and species.
Within the family Saltoposuchidae, Saltoposuchus occupies the basal position, while some analyses place Litargosuchus as the immediate sister to the Galahadosuchus-Terrestrisuchus clade.
